extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, peer reviewers, journal editors
extracted.subtask_short: writing peer reviews for academic papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting pre-publication peer review of academic manuscripts, emphasizing minimum-quality checks, honest scope-setting, mitigation of bias, and system-level tradeoffs for scalability and credentialing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify minimum scholarly criteria (the 'marketplace check')
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that minimum scholarly criteria are met (the marketplace check).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply field-appropriate minimum-quality checks to ensure a manuscript meets baseline scholarly standards (methodological adequacy, clarity, appropriate citation of prior work, etc.). This is a check that the work belongs in the community's marketplace of ideas rather than a guarantee of correctness or importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a credentialing signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide credentialing signal that the field can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat acceptance/publication as a community credential or canonization signal. Reviews and editorial decisions should convey whether the work meets the community's standards for inclusion, understanding that this signal is pragmatic rather than an absolute endorsement of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pretend to certify correctness or detect fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Not pretend to certify correctness or detect fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the limits of peer review: it 'can't even reliably detect fraud.' Reviewers should avoid language or claims that suggest the review has proven correctness or that fraud has been ruled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take the work seriously — read fully and avoid rubber-stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the work seriously rather than skim and rubber-stamp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from perfunctory, cursory reviews. The author notes that 'most scientists don't work hard at paper reviews,' so reviewers should actually read the manuscript, engage with arguments and evidence, and provide substantive feedback rather than a rubber-stamp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest about scope: a review sets a quality floor, not a guarantee
rubrics_metrics.description: Be honest that this is a quality floor — not a guarantee of truth or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly communicate the intended meaning of a positive review/acceptance: it indicates the work meets minimum standards, not that it is definitively correct, important, or fraud-free. This honesty helps set realistic expectations for credentialing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give fair consideration to disruptive or unexpected research
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review struggles with disruptive or unexpected research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that peer review tends to disfavour work that is unexpected or disruptive. Reviewers should take special care not to dismiss novel approaches merely because they challenge prevailing paradigms or the reviewer is unfamiliar with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate predictable reviewer biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers exhibit predictable biases (e.g., older reviewers can be dismissive of work that does not cite them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of systematic biases (self-citation expectations, status/reputational bias, conservatism toward new ideas) and actively mitigate them—declare conflicts, consider diverse reviewer perspectives, and evaluate ideas on substantive merits rather than personal or generational preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure reviewer diligence and effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Most scientists don't work hard at paper reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations for reviewers should include sufficient time and intellectual effort. Reviews should be conscientious: checking key claims, following key derivations or experiments as feasible, and providing concrete, actionable feedback rather than cursory judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tradeoffs for scalability: smaller trusted reviewer pools vs broad coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is fundamentally incompatible with scale; if we want it, we have to bring back elitism (smaller pool of trusted reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the system level, recognize a tradeoff between scalability and review quality. Options include limiting review to a smaller, more trusted set of reviewers (elitism) to maintain standards, or accepting diluted review quality if attempting mass-scale peer review; choose design and staffing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic expectations about peer review's ability to improve science
rubrics_metrics.description: The system 'completely fails to improve science and can't even reliably detect fraud.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overstate peer review's epistemic power: it is imperfect at improving scientific results and limited in fraud detection. Use peer review primarily for credentialing and baseline quality control rather than as the primary mechanism for correcting or improving scientific knowledge.
